1.pericope_label: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a thing was revealed unto Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar; and the thing was true, but the time appointed was long: and he understood the thing, and had understanding of the vision. In those days I Daniel was mourning three full weeks. I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all, till three whole weeks were fulfilled.

schools.summary: Place the chapter as the last and fullest revelation about the people's future, and read the appointed time as a warfare or tribulation rather than a span of years.
Fix the date by imperial chronology and by the political crisis behind it, the stopped rebuilding, and read the fast as preparation for prayer.
Summarise the vision's scope, identify the month and the river, and trace the mourning to the calamities foreseen for the nation's sins.
Takes the opening as a solemn attestation and measures the appointed time as sheer duration, reaching to Antiochus and in type beyond.

debates.question: How is the third year of Cyrus to be reckoned?

positions.position: From the death of the uncle with whom he had jointly reigned, when he became sole monarch of the whole Medo-Persian empire.
It answers to the first year of Darius the Mede.
From the conquest of Babylon, and so from the beginning of the prophet's subjection to that throne.

debates.question: Does the appointed time mean a long duration or a long warfare?

positions.position: Duration: as far as the end of the reign of Antiochus, three hundred years, and in type further still.
Warfare: the word means hardship or tribulation, and many contentions must pass before these things are accomplished.

outliers.claim: Rejects the guesses that the name Belteshazzar records an honour or commends his abilities, holding that the prophet used it to make the prophecy known where he was known by it, and to testify that a foreign name had not cut him off from the Church.
Qualifies the statement that he understood, arguing from a later chapter that the whole was not understood by him and that the duration of the tribulation was never clearly revealed.

themes: In the third year of Cyrus king of Persia a thing was revealed unto Daniel, whose name was called Belteshazzar; and the thing was true, but the time appointed was long: and he understood the thing, and had understanding of the vision.
In those days I Daniel was mourning three full weeks.
I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all, till three whole weeks were fulfilled.

4.pericope_label: And in the four and twentieth day of the first month, as I was by the side of the great river, which is Hiddekel; Then I lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and behold a certain man clothed in linen, whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz: His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.

schools.summary: Identify the stone, the river name and the parts of the figure with philological care, and insist the prophet was bodily present at the Tigris.
Treat the fast as preparation for prayer, weigh the proper name of the gold, and refuse to make the human form into a human nature.
Name the month and the river briefly and identify the appearance with Christ in royal and priestly robes.

debates.question: Who is the man clothed in linen?

positions.position: The Angel of God, God's Presence or Name, distinguished from Michael and from Gabriel: the One who was the Logos.
Very probably Christ, appearing in royal and priestly robes and in great brightness.
An angel: angels are called men only because God clothes them in that outward form, and it is a gross error to think they become men.

debates.question: What is the gold of Uphaz?

positions.position: The same as Ophir.
A place named only here and in one prophet, whose locality is unknown.
Not an epithet meaning pure, but the proper name of a region, on the strength of that prophet's usage.

outliers.claim: Reads the phrase for the feet strictly as the place where the feet are, inferring that the lower parts of the body and not the feet alone shone like burnished brass.

Lays out three competing identifications of the stone with the reason for each: beryl as sky-coloured, sardonyx as a flesh colour fitter for a human body, and chrysolite because the girdle made the body about it look golden.

themes: And in the four and twentieth day of the first month, as I was by the side of the great river, which is Hiddekel;
Then I lifted up mine eyes, and looked, and behold a certain man clothed in linen, whose loins were girded with fine gold of Uphaz:

His body also was like the beryl, and his face as the appearance of lightning, and his eyes as lamps of fire, and his arms and his feet like in colour to polished brass, and the voice of his words like the voice of a multitude.

7.pericope_label: And I Daniel alone saw the vision: for the men that were with me saw not the vision; but a great quaking fell upon them, so that they fled to hide themselves. Therefore I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me: for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength. Yet heard I the voice of his words: and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I in a deep sleep on my face, and my face toward the ground.

schools.summary: Measure the majesty of this appearance against the earlier one by the strength of the words used for the prophet's collapse, and press the question of what the companions perceived.
Treat the solitude of the seeing and the prostration as sanctions of the prophecy, and read the terror as a discipline that prepares for revelation.
Has the companions all feeling a divine influence while only the prophet saw the corporeal appearance.

debates.question: What did the prophet's companions perceive?

positions.position: They heard the voice but saw nothing, and the words spoken are nowhere recorded.
Only a confused sound, without understanding the language, since God meant to address one man alone.
A divine influence which they all felt, though only one saw the corporeal appearance.
Nothing at all: the opinion that they heard the voice is incorrect, since the voice was not heard until after they had fled.

outliers.claim: Reads the panic of the companions as wisely ordered, so that with them gone the prophet might be left alone to receive the secrets of the Lord.

Argues that God does not terrify his children because their disquiet delights him but because it profits them, since carnal feeling must be subdued and inborn perverseness makes that a violent business.

themes: And I Daniel alone saw the vision: for the men that were with me saw not the vision; but a great quaking fell upon them, so that they fled to hide themselves.
Therefore I was left alone, and saw this great vision, and there remained no strength in me: for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength.
Yet heard I the voice of his words: and when I heard the voice of his words, then was I in a deep sleep on my face, and my face toward the ground.

10.pericope_label: And, behold, an hand touched me, which set me upon my knees and upon the palms of my hands. And he said unto me, O Daniel, a man greatly beloved, understand the words that I speak unto thee, and stand upright: for unto thee am I now sent. And when he had spoken this word unto me, I stood trembling. Then said he unto me, Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words.

schools.summary: Trace the stages of recovery precisely, from the reeling on hands and knees to the standing upright, and identify the hand with the person who appeared.
Distinguish the touching hand from the glorious figure, and read the command not to fear as a bridling of fear rather than its removal.
Takes the hand as possibly God's own, since nothing was visible but a hand, and reads the visit as an answer to prayer.
Draws from the gradual recovery the rule that strength and comfort come by degrees, and that God makes his people sensible of weakness before he gives power.

positions.position: Not the figure whose hand was polished brass, but an attendant with a softer, more human hand, very probably Gabriel.
The hand of the person who appeared, spoken of as felt and not as seen.
Nothing was apparent but a hand, and since the hand often stands for God's power and majesty, perhaps God himself is meant.

outliers.claim: Turns the staged recovery into a rule of experience: those long cast down are helped up a little and then more, and the day of small things is not to be despised.
Holds that the angel meant not to abolish fear but to calm it, since fear is useful as a bridle while too great self-confidence breeds slothfulness and pride.

themes: And, behold, an hand touched me, which set me upon my knees and upon the palms of my hands.

And he said unto me, O Daniel, a man greatly beloved, understand the words that I speak unto thee, and stand upright: for unto thee am I now sent. And when he had spoken this word unto me, I stood trembling.
Then said he unto me, Fear not, Daniel: for from the first day that thou didst set thine heart to understand, and to chasten thyself before thy God, thy words were heard, and I am come for thy words.

13.pericope_label: But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia. Now I am come to make thee understand what shall befall thy people in the latter days: for yet the vision is for many days.

schools.summary: Identify the latter days with the Messianic world-time to which the coming vision stretches, and build the opposing prince into a doctrine of spiritual powers governing nations.
Argue the opposing prince is an evil spirit by eliminating the alternatives, and read the delay as proof that prayers may be heard while the answer is hidden.
Read the opposing prince as a human king whose hesitation or malice God overcame, and report the common identification of Michael with Christ.

debates.question: Who is the prince of the kingdom of Persia?

positions.position: An evil spirit: Satan or one of his chief officers, set to work mischief in the Persian court against the Jews.
Cyrus himself, who hesitated at the greatness of the work and resisted the secret inspirations sent him.
Cambyses, whose wicked counsels God suffered to prevail for a while.
One of the chief princes.
An archangel, the only one named in Scripture, whose name sometimes signifies the Messiah and sometimes the highest of that order.
Commonly supposed to mean Christ.

outliers.claim: Takes the whole verse as an answer to the complaint of delay, and draws from it that prayers may already be heard while the favour answering them is concealed, God caring for our safety in ways beyond our comprehension.
Corrects an interpreter who supposed the angel was referring to revelations already given, insisting the vision in view is the one still to come.

themes: But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia.
Now I am come to make thee understand what shall befall thy people in the latter days: for yet the vision is for many days.

15.pericope_label: And when he had spoken such words unto me, I set my face toward the ground, and I became dumb. And, behold, one like the similitude of the sons of men touched my lips: then I opened my mouth, and spake, and said unto him that stood before me, O my lord, by the vision my sorrows are turned upon me, and I have retained no strength. For how can the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord? for as for me, straightway there remained no strength in me, neither is there breath left in me. Then there came again and touched me one like the appearance of a man, and he strengthened me, And said, O man greatly beloved, fear not: peace be unto thee, be strong, yea, be strong. And when he had spoken unto me, I was strengthened, and said, Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me.

schools.summary: Describe the raising by degrees and the loss of speech and breath in exact terms, and hold the touching person to be the same throughout.
Read the prostration as reverence rather than despair, and the whole apparatus of touch and address as credentials distinguishing this prophecy from imposture.
Mark the change of posture and the dumbness, and name Gabriel as the one who restored the power of speech.

positions.position: Either Gabriel in a more manifest human form or another of the attendants, but not the man clothed in linen.
Gabriel.
The same person throughout, however much the wording seems to introduce another.

outliers.claim: Denies that the prostration can be ascribed to fear at all, since fear had already been driven away, and puts it down to reverence for the majestic person and gratitude for the answered prayer.

Explains the whole apparatus of touch and address as credentials, needed because Satan transforms himself into an angel of light, so that God marks this prediction off by fixed signs from his fallacies.

themes: And when he had spoken such words unto me, I set my face toward the ground, and I became dumb.

And, behold, one like the similitude of the sons of men touched my lips: then I opened my mouth, and spake, and said unto him that stood before me, O my lord, by the vision my sorrows are turned upon me, and I have retained no strength.
For how can the servant of this my lord talk with this my lord? for as for me, straightway there remained no strength in me, neither is there breath left in me.
Then there came again and touched me one like the appearance of a man, and he strengthened me,

And said, O man greatly beloved, fear not: peace be unto thee, be strong, yea, be strong. And when he had spoken unto me, I was strengthened, and said, Let my lord speak; for thou hast strengthened me.

20.pericope_label: Then said he, Knowest thou wherefore I come unto thee? and now will I return to fight with the prince of Persia: and when I am gone forth, lo, the prince of Grecia shall come. But I will shew thee that which is noted in the scripture of truth: and there is none that holdeth with me in these things, but Michael your prince.

schools.summary: Take the book as God's own record of history written beforehand, and read the adversative as encouragement rather than a warning of unrelieved calamity.
Identify the book with the eternal decree, arguing that God needs no books since he never forgets, and keep the opposing prince a spirit working in the Persian court.
Refer the book to revelations already given, keep the fight a struggle with a human king's reluctance, and make Michael the church's sole protector.

debates.question: What is the scripture of truth?

positions.position: The eternal and inviolable decree of God, called a book only by accommodation to human custom, since God never forgets and needs no books.
The revelations God had already conveyed or would shortly convey, including the earlier visions this prophet had written down.

debates.question: What is the fight the messenger returns to?

positions.position: A contest with the evil spirit of the Persian court, whose work slowed the building of city and temple.
The overcoming of the reluctance of Cyrus, whose decree no natural or political inclination can explain.
The providence that watched over Israel throughout the Persian sovereignty.
The opposing of mischievous designs.

outliers.claim: Makes Michael Christ himself, the sole protector of his church when all the princes of the earth desert or oppose it.

Reasons that since an angel can be in only one place at a time, one messenger or another had to be present with the Persian king by turns, then withdraws the argument on the ground that we know too little of the invisible world to affirm anything positively.

themes: Then said he, Knowest thou wherefore I come unto thee? and now will I return to fight with the prince of Persia: and when I am gone forth, lo, the prince of Grecia shall come.
But I will shew thee that which is noted in the scripture of truth: and there is none that holdeth with me in these things, but Michael your prince.
